formation.title: The Celtic Union
formation.text:
The impossible has been achieved. From the mist-shrouded shores of Brittany to the wind-swept Hebrides, from the green valleys of Wales to the stone walls of Connacht, the Celtic peoples stand united for the first time since the Romans drove them to the western edges of the world.

But unity is not uniformity. The Gaels and Brythons, the Cornish and Bretons, each bring their own laws, their own songs, their own way of war. The question now is what binds this union together: shared law and cultural kinship, allowing each nation its own character within a confederal embrace? Or the brotherhood of arms, a Celtic military tradition that has terrified empires from Rome to London?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Tir na Saor. We are bound by law, not the sword.

modifiers.name: Tir na Saor
modifiers.text: The Celtic Union is built not on conquest but on shared law. From the Brehon courts of Ireland to the cyfraith of Wales and the laws of the Bretons, the Celtic peoples have chosen confederation over subjugation, a land where each nation keeps its tongue and customs within a greater whole.

options.text: Claidheamh Mor. Let the Great Sword speak for all Celts.

modifiers.name: Claidheamh Mor
modifiers.text: The Great Sword is drawn. From Gallowglass axemen to Highland claymore-wielders, from Breton crossbowmen to Cornish tinners defending their mines, the Celtic peoples have forged a military brotherhood that turns every hillside into a fortress and every moor into a killing ground.

advances.name: Kern Warfare
advances.text: The ceithearnach, light skirmishing infantry armed with javelins, bows, and short swords, formed the backbone of Gaelic armies for centuries.

advances.name: Dun Fortification
advances.text: The Celtic tradition of hillforts and ringforts, from the great duns of Ireland to the brochs of Scotland, provided defensive strongholds across the landscape.

advances.name: Rundale System
advances.text: The rundale system of cooperative farming, where arable land was periodically redistributed among families, sustained Celtic agricultural communities.

advances.name: Cattle Economy
advances.text: In the Celtic world, wealth was measured in cattle. Great cattle fairs like Ballinasloe drew traders from across the islands.

advances.name: Brehon Tradition
advances.text: The Brehon legal system, based on arbitration and restitution rather than punishment, governed Irish society for over a millennium.

advances.name: Celtic Horsemanship
advances.text: The Celts were renowned horsemen since antiquity. The hobelar, a light cavalryman adapted to rough terrain, was a Celtic innovation adopted even by the English.

advances.name: Island Galleys
advances.text: The birlinn, the West Highland galley, was the warship of the Lords of the Isles and Hebridean chieftains, fast, maneuverable, and deadly in coastal waters.

advances.name: Monastic Learning
advances.text: Celtic monasteries at Iona, Clonmacnoise, and Bangor were centers of learning when much of Europe had forgotten how to read.

event.title: The Insular Art Revival
event.text:
The scriptoria of the Celtic monasteries have entered a new golden age. Master illuminators trained in the intricate knotwork patterns of the Book of Kells and the Lindisfarne Gospels are producing manuscripts of breathtaking beauty. But this is no mere antiquarian exercise, the monks have adapted their ancient techniques to new subjects: histories, legal codes, natural philosophy, and navigational charts.

The swirling interlace designs that once adorned only gospel pages now grace the halls of learning across the Celtic lands. From Iona to Clonmacnoise, from St. David's to the abbeys of Brittany, the Celtic scriptorium tradition proves that beauty and scholarship are inseparable.

options.text: The old art speaks with a new voice.

modifiers.name: Insular Art Revival
modifiers.text: A renaissance of Celtic manuscript illumination and artistic tradition enriches the cultural life of the union.

advances.name: Bardic Schools
advances.text: The bardic schools trained poets in the complex meters and genealogical knowledge required of a filid. A master bard held status equal to a king.

advances.name: Celtic Wool Trade
advances.text:
Scottish and Irish wool, processed through Cistercian monastic estates, was a prized export to the textile markets of Flanders.

Available in: Clachan

advances.name: Tanistry
advances.text: The Celtic system of succession by the most capable kinsman, rather than primogeniture, produced capable leaders but also succession disputes.

advances.name: Monastic Seafaring
advances.text: Celtic monks were remarkable voyagers. Saint Brendan's legendary navigation of the Atlantic reflects a real tradition of monastic seafaring in currachs.

advances.name: Atlantic Seamanship
advances.text: Celtic mariners mastered the treacherous Atlantic waters long before the Age of Sail, building ports and harbors from Galway to Brest.

advances.name: Fianna Tradition
advances.text: The Fianna were mythological warrior bands who lived in the wilderness, trained in arms and poetry alike. Their tradition inspired elite warband formations.

advances.name: Hedge Schools
advances.text: When penal laws banned Catholic and Irish-language education, the hedge school masters taught in secret, in fields, behind hedges, in barns, keeping learning alive.

advances.name: Mercenary Tradition
advances.text: Celtic warriors served as mercenaries across Europe for centuries, Gallowglass in Irish service, Scots in Swedish armies, Irish in French and Spanish regiments.

advances.name: Gaelic Lordship
advances.text: The consolidation of Gaelic lordships under the Celtic Union brings together the scattered tuatha into a coherent political structure.

advances.name: Cornish Mining
advances.text: Cornwall's tin and copper mines have been worked since the Bronze Age. Cornish mining expertise was exported across the world. The tinners smelt their black tin in blowing houses on the moor.

advances.name: Guerrilla Warfare
advances.text: The woodkern, forest-dwelling guerrilla fighters, perfected ambush tactics in the dense woods and bogs of the Celtic lands.

advances.name: Brehon Revival
advances.text:
The systematic revival and codification of Brehon law provides the Celtic Union with a legal tradition distinct from English common law.

Available in: Brehon Court

event.title: Codification of the Brehon Laws
event.text:
The ancient Brehon legal tradition, preserved through centuries of oral transmission and monastic copying, has now been systematically codified for the Celtic Union. Where English common law relied on precedent and royal authority, the Brehon system was built on arbitration, restitution, and communal consensus.

Scholars have gathered the scattered texts, the Senchus Mor, the Book of Aicill, the laws of hospitality and kinship, and harmonized them with Welsh cyfraith and Breton coutumes into a unified Celtic legal code. The Brehon courts now sit in every town, their judges trained in a tradition older than any parliament.

options.text: Let justice flow from the wisdom of our ancestors.

modifiers.name: Codified Brehon Law
modifiers.text: The systematic codification of Brehon law provides legal consistency across the Celtic Union.

advances.name: Language Revival
advances.text:
Organized efforts to preserve and promote Gaelic, Welsh, Breton, and Cornish, binding the Celtic peoples through their shared linguistic heritage. Scriptures, grammars and verse are set in type in the old tongues.

Available in: Scriptorium

advances.name: Celtic Trade League
advances.text: A pan-Celtic trading network linking the ports of Dublin, Glasgow, Cardiff, Brest, and Falmouth in mutual commercial advantage.

advances.name: Celtic Christianity
advances.text: Celtic Christianity, with its emphasis on monastic communities, peregrinatio, and local autonomy, offers a distinctive path between Rome and reform.

advances.name: Siege Resilience
advances.text: Centuries of defending against larger invaders have taught the Celtic peoples to make every hill and river crossing a deadly obstacle.

advances.name: Wild Geese Tradition
advances.text: The Wild Geese, Celtic soldiers who served in continental armies, bring back hard-won military expertise to their homeland.

event.title: Return of the Wild Geese
event.text:
For generations, the finest Celtic warriors sought service abroad, Irish regiments in the armies of France and Spain, Scottish mercenaries in Scandinavian service, Breton sailors under foreign flags. They called themselves the Wild Geese, exiles who dreamed of returning to a free Celtic homeland.

Now that dream is real. Veterans hardened by battles at Fontenoy, Cremona, and a dozen other continental engagements are streaming home. They bring with them not just martial skill but knowledge of foreign tactics, siege engineering, diplomatic connections, and intelligence networks cultivated across European courts. The question is how to employ them.

options.text: Form them into the Celtic Guard. Our finest soldiers return to fight.

modifiers.name: The Celtic Guard
modifiers.text: The returning Wild Geese form an elite guard corps, bringing continental military expertise to Celtic armies.

options.text: Their connections abroad are worth more than their swords.

modifiers.name: Eyes Across Europe
modifiers.text: The returning Wild Geese leverage their continental connections for diplomatic advantage and intelligence gathering.

advances.name: Smuggling Networks
advances.text: Celtic coastal communities developed extensive smuggling networks to evade English trade restrictions, moving goods through hidden coves and remote harbors.

advances.name: Constitutional Tradition
advances.text: Drawing on the Brehon legal tradition, Welsh cyfraith, and Enlightenment thought, the Celtic Union develops its own constitutional framework.

advances.name: Atlantic Fisheries
advances.text: The rich fishing grounds of the Celtic Sea and North Atlantic sustain coastal communities and provide a steady supply of experienced sailors. Pilchards and sardines are salted and pressed in the fish cellars of the coves.

advances.name: Linen Industry
advances.text: Irish and Scottish linen production, from flax cultivation to bleaching and weaving, becomes a major export industry. Beetling mills on the rivers give the web its close finish and sheen.

advances.name: Penal Resistance
advances.text: The experience of surviving centuries of penal legislation and cultural suppression has forged an unbreakable collective will.

advances.name: Industrial Heartlands
advances.text: Welsh coal and Scottish iron drive the Celtic industrial revolution, transforming the valleys and lowlands into workshops of the world.

advances.name: Literary Renaissance
advances.text: A flowering of Celtic-language literature, from the Ossianic poems to the Welsh eisteddfod tradition, inspires national consciousness.

advances.name: Cooperative Movement
advances.text: Building on ancient traditions of communal farming and mutual aid, the Celtic cooperative movement transforms banking and agriculture.

advances.name: Pan-Celtic Congress
advances.text: Delegates from all Celtic nations gather to coordinate policy, celebrate shared heritage, and present a united diplomatic front.

advances.name: Celtic National Army
advances.text: The professionalization of the Celtic military, drawing on generations of martial tradition from Gallowglass to Wild Geese.

destiny.name: Celtic Destiny
destiny.text: The Celtic Union stands united. Now begins the work of building a nation worthy of the name, whether through shared law and culture, or the strength of Celtic arms.

event.title: The Path Before Us
event.text:
The Celtic Union is no longer a dream whispered in smoky halls or sung in half-remembered ballads. It is real, a nation of nations stretching from Brittany to the Hebrides. But the harder work lies ahead. Any fool can raise a banner; it takes wisdom to build something that endures.

The elders and chieftains, the bards and lawmakers, the merchants and sailors, all look to us now. The choices we make in these first years will echo through centuries.

options.text: Let us build something that will outlast us all.

destiny.name: The Brehon Accord
destiny.text: Establish a unified legal code across all Celtic lands, embracing the ancient Brehon tradition of arbitration and restitution to bind the union's diverse peoples under shared law. Rennes, whose courts keep the written custom of Brittany, is held and built up.

conditions.text: Rennes is owned directly and has at least 31 development

event.title: The Brehon Accord
event.text:
From the hill of Tara to the courts of Rennes, the judges have spoken. A grand council of Brehon jurists, Welsh cyfreithwyr, and Breton coutumiers has produced something unprecedented: a unified Celtic legal code that honors the distinct traditions of each nation while binding them under common principles.

The Accord enshrines the old Celtic virtues, arbitration over punishment, restitution over revenge, the rights of the tuath alongside the authority of the ri. It is not an imitation of English common law or Roman civil law. It is something older, and perhaps something wiser.

options.text: The law is the sinew that binds our nations.

destiny.name: The Celtic Academy
destiny.text: Found a great center of learning that draws scholars from every Celtic nation, advancing knowledge for a modern confederation. Hold St Andrews, where the first university of Scotland was chartered, build it up to half again what it was, and found a library or a university there.

conditions.text: St Andrews is owned and has a Library or a University
St Andrews is owned directly and has at least 29 development

event.title: An Ollscoil Cheilteach
event.text:
The Celtic Academy has opened its doors. In a great hall that mingles the interlace patterns of Iona with the mathematical precision of the modern age, scholars from every Celtic nation gather to study, debate, and create.

But already a dispute has arisen about the Academy's purpose. Some argue it should focus on preserving and reviving the Celtic languages and arts, a bulwark against the cultural tide of larger neighbors. Others believe the Academy must look forward, embracing new sciences and practical knowledge to ensure the union's material prosperity.

options.text: Preserve our heritage. The languages come first.

modifiers.name: Guardians of the Tongue
modifiers.text: The Academy's focus on linguistic and cultural preservation strengthens Celtic identity, improving material output and tax revenues across the union.

options.text: Embrace the new sciences for a stronger union.

modifiers.name: The New Sciences
modifiers.text: The Academy's embrace of practical knowledge drives development and trade, though the rapid expansion invites minor inflationary pressures.

destiny.name: The Celtic Renaissance
destiny.text: Achieve a golden age of Celtic culture, a flowering of art, literature, and scholarship that proves the Celtic peoples are the equals of any civilization in Europe. Edinburgh, its city of printers and literary societies, is held and built up to twice what it was, and three in ten of the union's people can read.

conditions.text: Edinburgh is owned directly and has at least 51 development

event.title: Aisling na gCeilteach
event.text:
They call it the Celtic Vision, an Aisling made real. From the scriptoria of Clonmacnoise to the eisteddfodau of Wales, from the literary salons of Rennes to the music halls of Edinburgh, a cultural flowering is sweeping the Celtic lands that rivals any renaissance.

Poets compose in Gaelic and Brythonic with a confidence not seen since the age of the bards. Artists blend the ancient knotwork tradition with new techniques. Scholars publish works of philosophy, natural history, and mathematics that command respect across Europe.

The question now is how to direct this energy. The filid, the master poets who once held status equal to kings, argue for a return to the ancient bardic tradition where culture serves the nation's soul. The new intellectuals counter that culture must also serve commerce and practical innovation.

options.text: The filid tradition: culture as the soul of the nation.

modifiers.name: Voice of the Filid
modifiers.text: The revival of the bardic tradition extends Celtic diplomatic reach and heals the scars of past conflicts, streamlining governance.

options.text: The new learning: culture as the engine of progress.

modifiers.name: Engine of Progress
modifiers.text: The new learning transforms Celtic arts into commercial advantage, empowering merchants while sharpening military tactics.

destiny.name: The Celtic March
destiny.text: Reclaim the old Celtic territories of Cornwall and Cumbria from English control, pushing the borders of the union to their historic extent. The march is held by five Dun Forts.

conditions.text: Dun Forts stand in at least 5 owned locations

event.title: The Celtic March
event.text:
Celtic banners fly over Cornwall and Cumbria for the first time in centuries. The tin mines of Kernow and the mountain passes of the north are ours. In village squares across the newly liberated territories, people who had almost forgotten their Celtic heritage are relearning the old tongues, rediscovering the songs their grandmothers sang in secret.

The English called us savages. Let them look upon what savages can build.

options.text: The borders of the Celtic world grow wider.

destiny.name: Atlantic Dominion
destiny.text: Seize control of the northern seas by taking the Orkney Islands and establishing a foothold in Normandy, dominating the approaches to the Celtic heartland. Three harbours, Port Dunans or docks, shelter the fleets that keep them.

conditions.text: A Port Dunan or a port of the dock line (Dock, Dry Dock, Shipyard, Grand Shipyard, Naval Base) stands in at least 3 owned locations

event.title: Masters of the Northern Seas
event.text:
The Norse jarl of Orkney has bent the knee. Celtic ships patrol from the Pentland Firth to the Seine estuary. On the Normandy coast, our foothold gives us a voice in continental affairs that no English king can ignore.

The Celtic peoples have always been mariners. From Saint Brendan's legendary voyages to the birlinn fleets of the Hebridean lords, the Atlantic has been our highway. Now it is becoming our domain. The question is what to do with this mastery.

options.text: Build a war fleet to command these waters.

modifiers.name: Lords of the Waves
modifiers.text: A powerful Celtic war fleet dominates the northern seas, though the focus on naval construction slows the recovery of land forces.

options.text: Plant Celtic colonies across the Atlantic.

modifiers.name: Children of Brendan
modifiers.text: Following in the wake of the legendary monk-navigators, Celtic colonists spread across the Atlantic, building new communities in distant lands.

destiny.name: The Western Empire
destiny.text: Build a pan-Atlantic Celtic empire stretching from Iceland to Bordeaux, with London itself under Celtic rule, the final reversal of centuries of English domination. Dublin, seat of the high kingship, is held and built up to twice what it was.

conditions.text: Dublin is owned directly and has at least 58 development

event.title: Ard Ri na nIarthar
event.text:
London has fallen to Celtic arms. The city that for centuries was the seat of power that ground the Celtic nations underfoot is now a Celtic possession. From Reykjavik's volcanic shores to the vineyards of Bordeaux, from the Orkneys to the Thames, the Celtic Union commands an empire that stretches across the entire western seaboard of Europe.

The ancient bards prophesied this day, when the scattered children of the Celts would rise as one and reclaim what was taken from them. The high kingship, the Ard Ri, is no longer a title from legend. It is the reality of a people who refused to disappear.

options.text: Rule through strength. None shall challenge us again.

modifiers.name: The High King's Justice
modifiers.text: The Ard Ri rules through military supremacy, swift diplomacy, and the spoils of conquest.

options.text: Rule through prestige. Let the world acknowledge our greatness.

modifiers.name: The High King's Glory
modifiers.text: The Ard Ri commands through prestige and the loyalty of subject peoples, reducing the cost of asserting Celtic dominance.

units.name: Ceithearnach
units.text: Light skirmishing infantry armed with javelins and short swords. Fast and aggressive, the kern harried enemies with missile fire before closing to melee.

units.name: Birlinn
units.text: The West Highland galley, propelled by both sail and oar. Fast and maneuverable in coastal waters, the birlinn was the warship of the Hebridean lords.

units.name: Fianna
units.text: Elite warband infantry inspired by the mythological Fianna. These shock troops combine ferocious charges with iron discipline.

units.name: Woodkern
units.text: Forest-dwelling guerrilla fighters who excel at ambush and harassment in wooded and hilly terrain. The nightmare of every occupying army.

units.name: Wild Geese
units.text: Veterans of continental service, these battle-hardened soldiers combine Celtic martial ferocity with European tactical discipline.

units.name: Currach Raider
units.text: A fast, light vessel built for Atlantic coastal raiding. The currach tradition stretches back millennia, and these ships excel at blockading and harassing enemy shipping.

buildings.name: Dun Fort
buildings.text: A Celtic hillfort built on ancient defensive principles, commanding ground, thick stone walls, and provisions for a long siege.

buildings.name: Scriptorium
buildings.text: A monastic writing center in the insular tradition, producing illuminated manuscripts and educating the next generation of scholars.

buildings.name: Hedge School
buildings.text: A master and his scholars in a barn, a cabin by the ditch or the lee of a hedge. Reading, arithmetic, Latin and the old verse are taught for a fee of turf and meal, out of sight of the magistrates.

buildings.name: Rath Market
buildings.text: A traditional Celtic market and assembly ground at an ancient rath site, where cattle fairs, trade, and Brehon legal proceedings sustain the rural community.

buildings.name: Teach Ceoil
buildings.text: A House of Music where bards train in the ancient arts of poetry, genealogy, and musical composition, the cultural heart of Celtic civilization.

buildings.name: Clachan
buildings.text: A cooperative farming settlement organized under the rundale system, where families work shared lands and pool their livestock.

where.text: Wool is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Blowing House
buildings.text: The tinners' smelting house on a moorland stream. Black tin from the stream works is blown to white metal with charcoal and a water-driven bellows on the spot, so the tinners can work ground too poor to pay for carting the ore away. The tin ground it stands on yields more.

where.text: The location's raw material is Tin

buildings.name: Pilchard Cellar
buildings.text: The fish palace of a Cornish cove, the press of a Breton port. With a cellar ashore the seiners can take a whole shoal at once: the catch is laid in salt against the walls for a month, then packed in casks and pressed for the Lenten markets of the south. The fishery off its coast lands more.

where.text: The location's raw material is Fish

buildings.name: Beetling Mill
buildings.text: The last stage of linen. Rows of wooden beetles lifted by a water wheel pound the bleached web for days until the weave closes and takes a sheen. Where the mill and its bleach green stand, the farms around sow more flax for the linen trade.

where.text: The location's raw material is Fiber Crops

buildings.name: Port Dunan
buildings.text: A Celtic coastal harbor built for both commerce and war, sheltering birlinns and currachs in its protected anchorage.

buildings.name: Brehon Court
buildings.text: A court of law operating under the Brehon tradition, where trained jurists arbitrate disputes according to Celtic legal principles.

buildings.name: Ceardlann
buildings.text: A Celtic workshop of arts and learning where master craftsmen, scholars, and artists collaborate to produce works that blend ancient tradition with modern knowledge.

buildings.name: Ard Dun
buildings.text: A great Celtic high fortress commanding strategic approaches, built to withstand any siege and garrison the armies of the Western Empire.

list.name: Senchas Mar
list.text: The corpus of early Irish customary law composed in eighth-century Ulster and transmitted thereafter by hereditary legal families (the MacEgans of Connacht, the O'Davorens of the Burren, the MacClancys of Thomond) whose schools survived the twelfth-century reform of the Irish Church and continued in active use throughout the Gaelic lordships until the Stuart reconquest. The brehons functioned as arbitrators and chief advisors rather than judges in the modern sense, and were treated as neutrals in any conflict. Their judgements bound great and small alike but sat uneasily with seigneurial privilege.

list.name: Cyfraith Hywel
list.text: The Welsh law tradition codified at the synod of Hendy-gwyn-ar-Daf in the mid-tenth century under Hywel Dda, surviving in some forty manuscript lawbooks and in active use throughout the marcher lordships until the Acts of Union of 1535-1542. Welsh law divided society into five legal classes, recognized the rights of women in marriage and property to a degree exceptional in medieval Europe, and was administered by professional ynaid (judges) rather than churchmen, placing it in tension with the canon-law claims of the bishops.

list.name: Council of the Isles
list.text: The deliberative body of the Lordship of the Isles, which met on Eilean na Comhairle in Loch Finlaggan on Islay. Sixteen councillors: four great barons (Maclean of Duart, MacLeod of Harris, MacLeod of Lewis, Maclean of Loch Buie), four thanes (MacKinnon, MacNeil of Barra, MacNeil of Gigha, and one other), and four kinsmen of Clan Donald, with the Abbot of Iona and the Bishop of the Isles in attendance, issued land charters and pronounced judgements under the presidency of the MacDonald as Herdsman of the Isles. James IV sacked Finlaggan in 1493.

list.name: Aos Dana
list.text: The hereditary professional learned families of Gaelic Ireland and Scotland (filidh, seanchaidh, breithim, lucht ciuil) trained for seven to twelve years in the bardic schools that ran from November to May. By the mid-sixteenth century more than four hundred such families held tax-exempt land grants in return for their service to the ruling dynasties as poets, genealogists, jurists, physicians, and historians. The system collapsed with the Flight of the Earls in 1607 and the dispossession of Gaelic patronage.

list.name: Tanistry
list.text: The Gaelic elective succession of medieval Ireland and Scotland by which the tanaiste (heir-apparent and deputy) was chosen during the incumbent's lifetime from the derbfine, the four-generation kindred of eligible male agnates. The system favoured the proven warrior over the firstborn, producing capable rulers but also bitter dynastic feuds when rival branches of the same house each pressed their claim. Tanistry was preserved in Highland clan chiefship and Irish lordship until its formal abolition under James VI in 1607.

list.name: Coyne and Livery
list.text: The levy of free billeting and provender (Irish coinmheadh is buannacht) by which Gaelic and Hiberno-Norman lords sustained their kern, gallowglass, and horsemen on the populace: the single most important tax of late medieval Ireland. Coyne provided food and bedding to the lord's soldiers; livery provided fodder and stabling for their horses. The Tudor administration outlawed the practice as 'damnable' but it remained the indispensable foundation of Gaelic military power until the Plantations swept it away.

list.name: Stannary Charter
list.text: The Cornish tin-mining institution chartered by King John in 1201 and confirmed by Edward III in 1337 with the creation of the Duchy of Cornwall. Twenty-four stannators (six elected from each of the four stannaries of Tywarnhaile, Blackmoor, Foweymoore, and Penwith) met at Crockern Tor and at Truro to legislate over the tin-bounders, exempt from common taxes and from any jurisdiction save the Stannary Courts. Their parliament held a veto over Westminster acts affecting mining; suspended by Henry VII in 1496, it was restored by Charter of Pardon in 1508.
